newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FEATURE - CAUTIOUS HUNGARY SEEN AVOIDING CURRENCY TROUBLE.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - CAUTIOUS HUNGARY SEEN AVOIDING CURRENCY TROUBLE.

text.p: Hungary, preparing for European Union (EU) membership, will clear the first hurdle of economic reform by swinging to growth without currency difficulties faced elsewhere in the region, analysts say.

They add economic stability and a cautious foreign exchange liberalisation will protect the country's currency the forint from turbulence but also limit the inflow of short-term foreign speculative capital over the next few years.
Hungary, together with other central European states, has been invited by the EU for accession talks and is ambitious to meet monetary union (EMU) criteria for the longer term.
But before opening up its financial markets fully, the country has to overcome the initial difficulties of transition economies swinging to economic growth after years of recession.
THE KEY TO SUCCESS: STABILITY THEN GROWTH
Hungary launched an economic austerity programme in early 1995 to curb the budget and current account deficits which soared after artificially generated economic growth in 1994.
The programme, upon which the current economic policies are based on one slogan: stability then growth.
However, the austerity measures launched in 1995 cooled the economy and the gross domestic product increase remained well behind growth rates in other countries of the region.

The stress of economic policies began to shift from stability to growth from late 1996 after it became clear that inflation and external debt was steadily going down and the budget and the current account had stabilised.

Currently Hungary is moving at a different stage from the Czech Republic and Poland in what may be an economic cycle in central Europe: stabilisation leads to growth, but growth can lead to imbalances which then call for stabilisation.
Poland and the Czech Republic could be said to be on the second phase while Hungary is returning to the first.
TESTING THE CYCLE

Analysts said Hungary had the potential to break out of the cycle and generate growth without shocking the economy, as its structural reforms are the most advanced in the region, foreign investments continue to flow in with exports rising quickly.
The country's currency, which usually has the role of the thermometer in economies, hardly reacted to news of the Czech and Polish difficulties in the past few months.

"The fundamentals of the economy are so favourable that these will not create a speculation wave similar to what happened in the Czech Republic and Poland," National Bank of Hungary (NBH) Vice President Gyorgy Szapary said.

In a recent Reuters poll, the analysts' forecasts for the current account deficit averaged $2.19 billion for 1997 and $2.04 billion for 1998, compared with the government target of $2 billion for 1997 and $2 billion to $2.5 billion for 1998.

Many analysts agree with Szapary that the forint is unlikely to drift away permanently from the upper resistance level in the 4.5 percent wide intervention band, although analysts said the forint was likely to move down slightly.
"It will come down a little bit because as the economy picks up, the current account deficit will widen a little bit," London-based ING Barings analyst Nigel Rendell said.
"And we also think that due to the election in the early part of next year there will be a little bit of uncertainty in the market," he said. "But this is not a dramatic thing."
Rendell forecast the forint would go down to 209.00 to the dollar by the end of 1997 from the current 196.32, and to 222.00 by the end of 1998.

At the end of this year, the forint is likely to be one percent above the parity, still in the stronger half of the band, and by end-1998 it will go down to the centre of the intervention range, Rendell said.
CALCULABLE FORINT
Despite some uncertainties over the forint's position in the band and over the pace of decline in inflation, the forint will be a calculable currency, analysts said.
Hungary plans to maintain its crawling peg devaluation system, and to cut the monthly rate in line with the fall in inflation and the increase in productivity.
The current 1.1 percent monthly depreciation rate will be cut to one percent on August 15 and analysts said it may go down to 0.7 to 0.8 percent by end-1998 depending on inflation.
Hungary plans to cut inflation to some 18 percent in 1997 from 23.6 percent in 1996, and to 13.5 percent in 1998, while analyst forecasts average 18.46 and 14.63 percent respectively.

International organisations and analysts warned the government not to soften its fiscal policies before the 1998 elections and to agree a reasonable rise in real wages with employers and employees at talks to close in the autumn.

The NBH and analysts agree that the widening of the forint intervention band could enlarge the room for maneouvre of monetary policy, but there is no pressure for such a move, which would also carry the risk of appreciating the forint.
CAUTIOUS LIBERALISATION
The liberalisation of currency regulations is expected to continue next year, but only to a limited extent, with the restriction on short-term capital movements remaining in place.
Currently, foreigners are not allowed to buy Hungarian government securities with a shorter maturity than one year.

"We are still cautious," Judit Vadasz, head of the NBH regulatory department told Reuters, adding that press reports that the NBH may propose allowing foreigners to enter Hungary's currency futures markets were premature.
These restrictions are keeping forint trading turnover on Hungary's interbank foreign exchange market at low levels, at $150 to $250 million dollars a day, dealers and analysts said.
As a result of planned new legislation, foreign companies will be allowed to open branches in Hungary from next year.

Also Hungarians would be allowed to buy shares in all companies registered in OECD countries, as well as notes of OECD-based investment funds, and the NBH would also like to open the way for Hungarians to purchase real estate abroad.
Analysts said the NBH was right to lift some currency restrictions but retain others until they have to be abolished when Hungary becomes EU and EMU member.

"(The NBH) were afraid of a Mexico-type crisis (of a wave of short-term capital withdrawals) and the recent Czech crisis only reinforced their belief that their monetary policies were right," Bereczki said.
"While there is no political constraint, perhaps they do it well not opening up the market fully."
